papers.authors: Malek DA, Medeiros FA.

papers.title: Lipid-sensing GPR183-KRAS signaling mediates T H 17 autoimmunity and identifies fluvoxamine repurposing in uveitis.
papers.authors: Zhang C, Liu X, Xu N, Chen H, Gao Y, Gu C, Shen X, Wu J, Lu X, Zhang P, He Y, Xu Z, Su W.
papers.abstract: Autoimmune uveitis (AU) is a leading cause of irreversible blindness driven by pathogenic T helper 17 (T H 17) cell-mediated inflammation, yet current therapies are limited by efficacy and side effects, with immunometabolic mechanisms remaining poorly defined. By integrating single-cell RNA sequencing and multilayered metabolomic profiling in patients with AU and experimental AU models, we identified the lipid-sensing G protein-coupled receptor GPR183 as a key immunometabolic regulator in pathogenic CD4 + T cells. Upon activation, GPR183 modulates intracellular signaling via suppression of cyclic adenosine monophosphate-cAMP-dependent protein kinase activity and promotion of son-of-sevenless-dependent KRAS activation, which in turn elicits copper overload-induced mitochondrial oxidative stress, structural impairment, and metabolic rewiring toward glycolysis, thereby promoting T H 17 cell pathogenicity. For clinical translation, virtual screening of Food and Drug Administration-approved drugs coupled with molecular docking and microscale thermophoresis validation identified fluvoxamine (FLV) as a direct GPR183 antagonist. In in vivo and in vitro uveitis and colitis models, FLV attenuated GPR183-KRAS signaling, dampened pathogenic T H 17 cell responses, and alleviated tissue inflammation. These findings delineate a unique GPR183-KRAS-mitochondrial damage axis governing T H 17-driven autoimmunity and support repurposing FLV as a translatable therapeutic approach for AU and other autoimmune inflammatory disorders.

papers.title: Cellular-resolution three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) of neuronal population activity at 2-mm depth in the mammalian brain.
papers.authors: Santra K, Barber K, Logiacco F, Frechou MA, Bellafard A, Liou JY, Vaziri A.
papers.abstract: Extending the depth reach of multiphoton microscopy for imaging neuronal population activity in the scattering mammalian brain is an 'exponentially hard' problem. Three-photon (3p) microscopy has enabled imaging of neuroactivity at depths up to ~1.2 mm in the mouse brain; however, the fundamental depth limit of 3p imaging, as set by the depth at which out-of-focus background fluorescence exceeds the in-focus fluorescence signal, is well beyond 2 mm. Reaching this fundamental depth limit in 3p imaging has been hampered by insufficient in-focus fluorescence signal. Here we demonstrate a three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) system that approaches this fundamental depth limit via systematic and principled optimization of the in-focus fluorescence signal. TrUDI matches the parameters of the excitation laser, the optical system, and the acquisition to linear and nonlinear limits for safe laser exposure while satisfying the spatiotemporal requirements of single-cell resolution calcium (Ca 2+ ) imaging. TrUDI achieves a ~250-fold increase in detected fluorescence photon yield at the same laser power as in previous approaches thereby enabling in vivo cellular-resolution recordings of neuronal population activity within fields of view of ~230 × 230 µm 2 at 8.6 Hz at tissue depths of up to ~2 mm in mouse cortex and hippocampus.

papers.title: Population-scale single-nucleus multi-omic profiling of skeletal muscle reveals extensive context-specific genetic regulation.
papers.authors: Varshney A, Manickam N, Orchard P, Tovar A, Ventresca C, Zhang Z, Feng F, Mears J, Erdos MR, Narisu N, Nishino K, Rai V, Stringham HM, Jackson AU, Tamsen T, Gao C, Yang M, Koues OI, Welch JD, Burant CF, Williams LK, Jenkinson C, DeFronzo RA, Norton L, Saramies J, Lakka TA, Laakso M, Tuomilehto J, Mohlke KL, Kitzman JO, Koistinen HA, Liu J, Boehnke M, Collins FS, Scott LJ, Parker SCJ.
papers.abstract: Skeletal muscle tissue underlies several polygenic metabolic traits and diseases. Identifying their genetic mechanisms requires pinpointing cell types, regulatory elements, target genes and causal variants. Here we use genetic multiplexing to generate population-scale single-nucleus chromatin accessibility (single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin using sequencing (snATAC-seq)) and transcriptome (single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq)) maps across 287 frozen human skeletal muscle biopsies. We identify 13 cell types and integrate genetic variation to discover >7,000 expression quantitative trait loci (eQTLs) and >100,000 chromatin accessibility QTLs (caQTLs) across cell types, including context-specific eQTL/caQTL with significant G × C interaction. We identify nearly 2,000 eGenes colocalized with caQTL and construct causal directional maps for chromatin accessibility and gene expression. Almost 3,500 genome-wide association study (GWAS) signals across 38 relevant traits colocalize with sn-eQTL/caQTL, most in a cell-specific manner. These signals typically colocalize with caQTL and not eQTL, highlighting the importance of population-scale chromatin profiling for GWAS functional studies. The results of this study illuminate the genetic regulatory architecture of human skeletal muscle.

papers.title: Spatial and sectoral water demand assessment for the African continent.
papers.authors: Vanham D, Gunathilake D, Gunasekara B, Tilahun S, Brouziyne Y, Zimale FA, Rawat M, Vanham R, El Hafyani M, Thowfeek A, Kumarasinghe S, Vaca-Jiménez SD, Gerbens-Leenes PW, Langan S.
papers.abstract: Water demand is the volume of water required by a sector to satisfy its needs 1,2 . Across Africa, these demands are frequently unmet 3 , yet their spatial and sectoral distribution remains incompletely characterized, limiting informed water-management decisions 4 . Here, we provide an Africa-wide estimate of water demand for 2020 across six sectors and multiple subsectors at high spatial resolution. Because the analysis integrates heterogeneous datasets and modelling assumptions, the resulting values should be interpreted as harmonized estimates rather than direct observations of realized water use. We estimate total annual water demand at 347 km 3 , comprising 60 km 3 (17%) for municipalities (57-64 km 3 , with ±20% key parameters variations), 225 km 3 (65%) for irrigation (214-233 km 3 , 95% confidence interval, with ±20% variations in irrigation efficiency), 11 km 3 (3%) for livestock, 15 km 3 (4%) for manufacturing, 33 km 3 (10%) for electricity including hydropower and 3 km 3 (1%) for mining (3-4 km 3 , with annual production variations). Estimated demand increased by 26% between 2010 and 2020. The dominant water-demand sector varies across regions and river basins, broadly reflecting established geographical and socioeconomic patterns. In parts of northern and southern Africa, estimated demand exceeds water availability, although results depend on assumptions regarding environmental-flow protection 5 . Elsewhere, water availability exceeds aggregate demand despite limited access to piped drinking water, indicating that physical availability alone does not determine water security. Our analysis therefore provides a spatially and sectorally resolved baseline for identifying water-demand pressures and access constraints rather than establishing a new causal mechanism of water insecurity. Local estimates should be interpreted cautiously given uncertainties in the underlying datasets.

papers.title: Emotion regulation capacity lacks a shared neural signature.
papers.authors: Sicorello M, Zaehringer J, Kraynak TE, Gianaros PJ, Nebe S, Paschke LM, Steimke R, Stelzel C, Walter H, LaBar KS, Graner JL, Kim SH, Wessa M, Sandner M, Weinmar F, Derntl B, Huneke NTM, Fagan HA, Fernández G, Yan L, Marín-Morales A, Verdejo-Román J, Steward T, Harrison BJ, Davey CG, Dörfel D, Neta M, Pierce J, Stolz DS, Kissler J, Benzait A, Erk S, Berboth S, van Reekum CM, Tupitsa E, Bratec SM, Sorg C, Müller-Pinzler L, Sokołowski A, Dragan WŁ, Folkierska-Żukowska M, Jentsch VL, Merz CJ, Scheffel C, Diers K, Nashiro K, Min J, Mather M, Heinke S, Gärtner A, McRae K, Powers JP, Doren N, Maier SU, Dziobek I, Guendelman S, Gaebler M, Daniels JK, Burghart M, Schmidt SNL, Hofhansel L, Habel U, NIDER Consortium, Kohn N, Morawetz C.
papers.abstract: Cognitive reappraisal refers to changing how one thinks about a situation to alter its emotional impact. It is central to well-being 1 and engages prefrontal regulatory circuits 2 , prompting the assumption that their activity reflects a person's capacity to regulate emotions 3-5 . Yet evidence for this assumption remains inconclusive and has not been established at scale. Here we analysed 40 task-based functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) datasets in a preregistered consortium with 2,175 participants and show that three widely used indicators of reappraisal capacity-trait questionnaires, task-based affective ratings and amygdala down-regulation-do not converge on a common core. Moreover, none of the three indicators showed the expected association with canonical prefrontal regulatory circuits. Trait questionnaires showed no detectable neural associations across the brain and task-based affective ratings were instead associated with responses in the amygdala and sensorimotor cortices. At the process level, canonical control circuits were engaged during both emotion generation and reappraisal, challenging their presumed specificity for emotion regulation. These findings caution against using activation in putatively regulatory brain regions to infer how well a person regulates emotions, with implications for neural biomarkers, interventions and psychoeducation that link emotion regulation difficulties to specific regional brain deficits.

papers.title: SWI/SNF complexes shape 3D chromatin architecture through CTCF and cohesin.
papers.authors: Debek S, Meydan C, Chin CR, Yu J, Durmaz C, Tsialta I, Pelzer B, Maurer C, Ou A, Laguillo-Diego A, Scourzic L, Tumuluru S, Teater M, Wu R, Darsow B, Rivas MA, Marin-Rubio JL, Stadtfeld M, Apostolou E, Mason CE, Elenitoba-Johnson KSJ, Risca VI, Melnick A, Barisic D.
papers.abstract: The BAF (also known as mammalian SWI/SNF) chromatin remodelling complexes are essential regulators of nucleosome positioning and transcription factor binding 1,2 . Loss-of-function (LOF) mutations in genes encoding components of the BAF complexes are among the most frequent across cancer types 3 . However, a unifying mechanism that explains their widespread disruption remains unclear. Here we disrupted BAF function through pharmacological inhibition and ARID1A deletion across various mammalian cell types and tissues and observed a conserved chromatin response: increased accessibility at CTCF-binding sites. ARID1A LOF alone was sufficient to drive these changes, which demonstrates that canonical BAF (cBAF) disruption is the key driver of CTCF gain. Genomic profiling showed increased CTCF and SMC3 occupancy, which reveals an antagonistic relationship between cBAF and CTCF-cohesin complexes. Furthermore, cBAF loss restructured 3D genome organization, which led to a strengthening of topologically associating domain boundaries and subdivision of large domains into smaller insulated structures. Long-range enhancer-promoter loops were replaced by shorter, promoter-proximal loops anchored at CTCF-enriched sites. To determine how CTCF function is enabled following cBAF loss, we profiled CTCF-interacting cofactors and found that CTCF binds directly to fully assembled PBAF. After cBAF depletion, PBAF was recruited to sites of increased CTCF occupancy, which demonstrates that there is an antagonistic switch between SWI/SNF subcomplexes. In vivo, conditional Arid1a deletion in primary mouse cells resulted in the expansion of a highly proliferative population marked by elevated accessibility at CTCF sites. This phenotype was fully reversed by either Ctcf or Pbrm1 deletion, which establishes that cBAF and the activity of CTCF and PBAF have contrasting roles.

papers.title: MCT1-dependent mitochondrial lactate import sustains cardiac metabolism.
papers.authors: Cluntun AA, Visker JR, Velasco-Silva JN, Carrington J, Cedeño-Rosario L, Napoli GC, Kim JE, Shankar TS, Brothwell MJ, Hamouche R, Narbona-Pérez ÁJ, Ling J, Toshniwal AG, Low HK, Cunningham CN, Eberhardt DR, Li J, Stanley CE, Alcantara QA, Yadav T, Maves RL, Swiatek WI, Offei NA, Blaze B, Shetty SP, Chaudhuri D, Hong T, Rothstein JD, Muoio DM, Paulo JA, Gygi SP, Tseliou E, Navankasattusas S, Cox JE, Funai K, Drakos SG, Rutter J, Ducker GS.
papers.abstract: The heart possesses a dynamic capacity to oxidize a variety of fuels, including glucose and lactate, to meet its energetic demands under diverse dietary, exertion and injury stressors 1 . Oxidation of carbohydrate substrates is thought to converge on the cytosolic generation of pyruvate, which is transported by the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC) for entry into the tricarboxylic acid cycle 2 . Here we find that glucose-derived carbon is oxidized in mouse myocardium even when the MPC is genetically ablated. Using genetic and pharmacological tools, we demonstrate that lactate monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1, encoded by Slc16a1) is required for the oxidation of glucose carbon by MPC-deficient myocardium. We further observe that MCT1, traditionally localized to the plasma membrane, also resides in the inner mitochondrial membrane of mouse and human cardiomyocytes. Together with matrix-localized LDHB, MCT1 enables mitochondrial lactate conversion to pyruvate and NADH, directly fueling the electron transport chain. Loss of MCT1 impairs lactate oxidation, disrupts metabolic flexibility and accelerates the development of heart failure with increased mortality after hyperactivation of the neurohormonal axis or ischemia-reperfusion injury. Thus, the existence of a parallel lactate-based pathway for carbohydrate oxidation can sustain cardiac energetics and maintain myocardial structure and function under diverse stress conditions.

papers.title: Connectome simulations identify a central pattern generator for fly walking.
papers.authors: Pugliese SM, Chou GM, Abe ETT, Turcu D, Lancaster JK, Tuthill JC, Brunton BW.
papers.abstract: Animal locomotion relies on rhythmic body movements driven by central pattern generators (CPGs): neural circuits that produce oscillating output without oscillating input. However, the circuit structure of a CPG for walking is not known in any animal 1,2 . To identify the cells and synapses that underlie rhythmic leg movement in walking flies, we developed dynamic simulations of the Drosophila ventral nerve cord connectomes 3-6 . A computational activation screen of descending neurons from the central brain identified DNg100-a known command neuron for walking-as the strongest driver of rhythmic leg motor activity. Simulated network pruning isolated a minimal rhythm-generating circuit consisting of one inhibitory and two excitatory interneurons; this three-neuron circuit was necessary and sufficient for motor rhythms across all six legs and in four connectome datasets. Simulations also predicted that a separate descending pathway (DNb08) drives rhythmic leg movements, which we confirmed experimentally using optogenetics in behaving flies. Our results reveal the cellular identity and synaptic structure of a putative CPG circuit for walking and other rhythmic leg movements in flies.

papers.title: Tumour assembloids recapitulate tumour-CAF-T cell crosstalk in renal cancer.
papers.authors: Kim E, Kang M, Han JH, Lee J, Kim Y, Jeong CW, Lee H, Kim HJ, Shin K.
papers.abstract: Dynamic interactions between tumours and their microenvironment are crucial for cancer progression and therapeutic outcomes 1,2 . However, our understanding of these relationships remains limited by the constrained capacity of current human model systems to manipulate diverse cellular components and to interrogate complex tumour-stroma crosstalk. Here we generated combinatorial, mix-and-match tumour assembloids by conditionally reconstituting multiple components of human renal cell carcinoma, including cancer cells, cancer-associated fibroblasts (CAFs) and tumour-infiltrating immune cells. Using genetically engineered renal cell carcinoma assembloids with humanized mouse models, we uncovered mechanisms by which CAFs coordinate interactions between tumour cells and CD8 + T cells to maintain non-cell-autonomous CD8 + T cell stemness and drive responsiveness to anti-PD-1 therapy. These interactions operate through a tumour-CAF-T cell signalling axis in which tumour-derived WNT induces CAF expression of activin A, which enhances CD8 + T cell stemness and sensitivity to PD-1 blockade. In non-responders, we also identified a subset of WNT-unresponsive CAFs that do not produce activin A, which leads to impaired CD8 + T cell stemness and resistance to therapy. Together, these findings establish a tumour-CAF-T cell axis as a key determinant of heterogeneous responses to immune checkpoint inhibitors. Moreover, tumour assembloids provide a versatile platform for mechanistic dissection of the tumour microenvironment and evaluation of personalized immunotherapy strategies.

papers.title: Monolithically and in situ integrated PbS infrared imagers.
papers.authors: Li S, Liu J, Gao L, Wang Y, Liu R, Wan J, Li S, Li Z, Tang J, Ma L, Liu M, Lin C, Ji X, Liu Y, Chen C, Su X, Li L, Zhang J, Luo J, Tang J.
papers.abstract: Image sensors are critical components in artificial intelligence 1-3 , yet conventional approaches bond detector arrays to readout integrated circuits (ROICs), a process that increases complexity and cost 4 . The ideal alternative-growing the detector directly on the ROIC from solution using raw materials-has remained elusive owing to the difficulty in achieving electronic-grade films through a ROIC-compatible process 5,6 . Here, inspired by biomineralization principles 7 , we demonstrate monolithic in situ integration (MISI) of high-performance lead sulfide (PbS) photodetectors on ROICs by means of a room-temperature aqueous process. By regulating Pb-OH complexation and suppressing environmental perturbations, we achieve quasi-single-crystalline PbS films with excellent electronic properties (carrier density approximately 2 × 10 15 cm -3 , mobility 124 cm 2 V -1 s -1 ) and wafer-scale, pixel-level uniformity. Through antimony doping, the resulting photodiodes exhibit a record specific detectivity of 4.4 × 10 11 Jones at 2.5 µm, surpassing commercial InGaAs detectors 8 . We further fabricate a 640 × 512-pixel focal-plane array that captures clear infrared images and also integrate devices directly onto flexible ROICs. This solution-based MISI approach offers a scalable and transformative route for advanced optoelectronics and sensors.

papers.title: Rare and common genetic variants shape single-cell immune gene expression.
papers.authors: Cuomo ASE, Spenceley E, Tanudisastro HA, Bowen B, Henry A, Huang HL, Xue A, Zhou W, Welland MJ, Bryen SJ, Dong OA, Lee AS, Pullin JM, Wing K, Tang O, Gray MP, Franklin M, Harper M, Silk M, Bobowik K, Stuckey A, Marshall J, Bakiris V, Uren C, McCloy RA, Madala BS, Miniter A, Bartie C, Neavin DR, Qiao Z, Ben-David E, Chen L, Farh KK, Grieve SM, Nguyen T, Wallace C, Piscionere J, Siggs OM, Nicholas H, de Lange KM, Hewitt AW, Figtree GA, MacArthur DG, Powell JE.
papers.abstract: Understanding the genetic basis of gene expression can shed light on the regulatory mechanisms underlying complex traits and diseases 1,2 . Single-cell-resolved measures of RNA levels and single-cell expression quantitative trait loci have revealed genetic regulation that drives cell states and types across diverse tissues 3 . Here we describe phase 1 of TenK10K, which leverages single-cell RNA sequencing data from more than 5 million cells across 28 immune cell types, along with matched whole-genome sequencing data from 1,925 individuals. This provides power to detect associations for rare and low-frequency genetic variants that have largely been uncharacterized in their impact on cell-specific gene expression. We map the effects of both common and rare variants in a cell-type-specific manner using a recent method that increases power by modelling single cells directly rather than aggregated 'pseudobulk' counts. We identify putative common regulatory variants for 83% of all 21,404 genes tested and cumulative rare-variant signals for 47% of those genes. We explore how genetic effects vary across cell types and states, develop a framework to determine the degree of single-cell expression quantitative trait loci cell-type specificity and show that about half of the effects are observed only in one or a few cell types. By integrating our results with functional annotations and disease information, we further characterize the likely molecular modes of action for many disease-variant associations. Finally, we explore the effects that genetic variants have on gene expression across continuous cell states, and effects that vary cell-state abundance directly.

papers.title: Eukaryotes' closest relatives are internally simple syntrophic peptidotrophic archaea.
papers.authors: Imachi H, Nobu MK, Ishii S, Hashiguchi H, Hirakata Y, Hosogi N, Ikuta T, Isaji Y, Miyata M, Miyazaki M, Morono Y, Murata K, Nakagawa S, Narita A, Ogawara M, Okada S, Saito Y, Sakai S, Shimamura S, Tahara YO, Takaki Y, Takano Y, Tasumi E, Uematsu K, Yoshimura T, Takai K.
papers.abstract: Eukaryotes are theorized to have an origin associated with the archaeal phylum Promethearchaeota (formerly Asgard archaea) 1-3 . The first cultured representatives revealed valuable insights 4,5 but are still distantly related to eukaryotes, leaving many unknowns regarding eukaryogenesis. Here we report the isolation of two strains, HC1 and SC1, that belong to the archaeal lineage that branches closest to eukaryotes (Heimdallarchaeia); 6-8 these isolates are members of a pure co-culture and a tri-culture with methanogenic partners. Both are obligately anaerobic, syntrophic, peptide-degrading and mesophilic archaea that produce protrusions and vesicles but lack persistent internal membrane structures, like Promethearchaeales 4,5 . All Promethearchaeota isolates demonstrate behaviour focused on cell construction and membrane structures rather than division, in contrast to typical prokaryotes 9 . Strain HC1 possesses genes associated with aerobic lifestyles (such as cytochrome c oxidase (Cox)) but co-cultures cannot grow under (micro)oxic conditions. Meanwhile, the strain demonstrates growth under microoxic conditions when in the presence of aerobes, suggesting that Cox supports oxygen detoxification rather than respiration. Comparative genomics provides evidence that, like HC1, Cox-possessing Heimdallarchaeia studied to date probably do not respire oxygen. The wide conservation of anaerobiosis, cell structure without persistent intracellular membranes and membrane protrusions across Promethearchaeota suggest that the archaeal ancestor of eukaryotes may have had such physiological features. In this cultivation-informed scenario for eukaryogenesis, the archaea-eukaryote transition would involve a steep transition in cell structure and physiological shift from anaerobiosis to (facultative) aerobiosis 10 , with early interactions between the archaeal host and mitochondrial ancestor probably occurring under low-oxygen conditions and at least partially mediated by oxygen detoxification.

papers.title: Presynaptic homeostasis mediated by exocytosis of a SNARE protein.
papers.authors: Xu H, Rao L, Edwards RH.
papers.abstract: The neural plasticity that underlies adaptation and learning requires countervailing homeostatic mechanisms to maintain the stability and responsiveness of neural circuits. Previous work has described several forms of synaptic homeostasis 1 , but the mechanisms that detect changes in activity and transduce these into altered neurotransmission have remained poorly understood. Here we show that high-frequency stimulation alters the subsequent properties of neurotransmitter release to confer a presynaptic form of homeostasis, independent of postsynaptic receptors. The mechanism involves vesicular SNARE protein (v-SNARE) VAMP7 (vesicle-associated membrane protein 7), which reduces neurotransmitter release by inhibiting the entry of Ca 2+ specifically through P/Q-type presynaptic Ca 2+ channels. Previous work has implicated target SNARE proteins (t-SNAREs) in the inhibition of Ca 2+ channels 2 , but without clear physiological rationale. We show that the activity-dependent regulation of release mediated by VAMP7 requires the t-SNARE syntaxin. Although VAMP7 acts at the plasma membrane to inhibit P/Q-type channels, it localizes predominantly to a subset of synaptic vesicles made by adaptor protein-3 (AP-3) that respond specifically to high-frequency stimulation 3,4 . The localization of VAMP7 to AP-3-derived synaptic vesicles thus provides a mechanism for the activity-dependent delivery of VAMP7 to the plasma membrane, where it associates with syntaxin to inhibit P/Q-type Ca 2+ channels and transmitter release. This homeostatic form of metaplasticity operates at multiple excitatory synapses, and in its absence, the fraction of FOS + neurons increases several fold, revealing a general property of excitatory neurotransmission that might also maintain the sparsity of neural connections.

papers.title: Delayed electron-hole recombination in a pseudo-direct semiconductor.
papers.authors: Righetto M, Banerjee D, Jia Z, Lilly JRS, Lim VJ, Lal S, Yan S, Lee JE, Patel JB, Johnston MB, Lin Q, Filip MR, Herz LM.
papers.abstract: Kirchhoff demonstrated the reciprocity between absorptivity and emissivity for blackbody radiation in 1860 (ref. 1 ), thereby establishing the general principle that a good absorber must also be a good emitter. This principle underpins the generalized Planck's law 2 and, when applied to semiconductors-in the form of the van Roosbroeck-Shockley equation 3 -results in substantial limitations to solar energy conversion. Here we demonstrate how this reciprocity can be circumvented in semiconductors, such as bismuth sulfide, showing a pseudo-direct bandgap character-that is, featuring a lower-energy indirect transition paired with a direct transition placed a few k B T above. After determining the pseudo-direct bandgap nature of bismuth sulfide, we reveal how this feature substantially retards bimolecular electron-hole recombination in this material with respect to classic direct semiconductors 4 . The resulting combination of a high absorption coefficient and delayed recombination offers the unprecedented possibility of overcoming limitations associated with Planck's law, with far-reaching potential for solar energy conversion.

papers.title: Perinatal elimination of genetically aberrant human cortical neurons.
papers.authors: Shao DD, Zhao Y, Brew J, Adla Y, Ghosh U, Viswanadham VV, Luquette LJ, Zhao S, Kriz AJ, Qian X, Taketomi T, Coy S, Santagata S, Miller M, Tsuruta F, Park PJ, Walsh CA.
papers.abstract: Human neurons are postmitotic and long-lived, requiring precise genomic regulation. Normal neuronal function is highly dosage-sensitive, with copy number variants (CNVs) and heterozygous point mutations associated with a host of neurodevelopmental and neuropsychiatric conditions 1-4 . Here we investigated somatic CNVs arising in single neurons to understand the dynamic processes that shape the normal neuronal genetic landscape. Altogether, we sequenced 2,357 single neurons from human postmortem brain from fetal to postnatal life. Two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches-Tn5-transposase-based amplification (1,526 neurons, 16 individuals) and primary template amplification 5 (831 neurons, 12 individuals)-showed that an average of 25.9% [12.7-46%] of prenatal cortical neurons have highly aberrant genomes, that is, widespread CNVs involving multiple chromosomes. This proportion reduced by about 4.5-fold after birth across the two single-cell whole-genome sequencing approaches (Fisher meta-analysis P = 3.5 × 10 - 6 ). Neurons with widespread CNVs were mainly eliminated perinatally, timed roughly parallel to periods of programmed cell death 6 , whereas neurons with smaller CNV burdens declined slowly in frequency with postnatal age. CNVs in surviving neurons were depleted for dosage-sensitive genes and genes involved in neurodevelopmental disorders (hypergeometric test P < 0.05), suggesting selective elimination of neurons with these CNVs. Analysis of 44,861 nuclei with single-nucleus assay for transposase-accessible chromatin (snATAC) and single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) showed that neurons with high CNV burdens exhibited abnormal synaptic gene expression, suggesting that abnormal synaptic gene regulation contributes to neuronal elimination. Elimination of defective neuronal genomes might represent an important developmental genome quality-control process that may be vulnerable in neurodevelopmental disease, and suggests purifying selection during human neurodevelopment.

papers.title: Interpretable models for scRNA-seq data embedding with multi-scale structure preservation.
papers.authors: Novak D, de Bodt C, Lambert P, Lee JA, Van Gassen S, Saeys Y.
papers.abstract: The ability to explore high-dimensional single-cell transcriptomics data efficiently is crucial in many biological studies. Dimensionality reduction techniques have therefore emerged as a basic building block of analytical workflows. They generate low-dimensional embeddings that capture important structures in the data and are often used in discovery, quality control, and downstream analysis. However, the trustworthiness of current methods and the rigor of popular evaluation criteria are limited. We tackle this in an empirical study of structure-preserving data embeddings, delivering two tools. First, we introduce ViScore: a robust scoring framework that improves both unsupervised and supervised quality metrics, with emphasis on scalability and fairness. Second, we introduce ViVAE: a deep-learning model that achieves better multi-scale structure preservation and is equipped with new tools for interpretability. We demonstrate the potential of these contributions to advance the trustworthiness of single-cell dimensionality reduction in a quantitative comparison and focused case studies.

papers.title: Deep Lineage: Single-cell lineage tracing and fate inference using deep learning.
papers.authors: Sadria M, Zhang A, Lai HG, Bader GD.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in single-cell RNA sequencing and lineage tracing techniques have provided valuable insights into the temporal changes in gene expression during development, tumor progression, and disease onset. However, there are few computational methods available to analyze this information to help understand multicellular dynamics. We introduce Deep Lineage, a deep-learning method for analyzing time-series single-cell RNA sequencing with matched lineage tracing data. Our method accurately predicts early cell fate biases and gene expression profiles at different time points within a clone, surpassing existing methods in fate prediction accuracy. We further validate our model using LineageSim, a fate-aware lineage simulator, demonstrating robustness to technical noise such as barcode dropout and clone misidentification. Additionally, we apply Deep Lineage to in silico perturbations in cellular reprogramming and hematopoiesis to identify key genes and pathways associated with cell fate determination and propose testable perturbation hypotheses for experimental follow-up.

papers.title: Multimodal spatial transcriptomics redefines cortical pathology in Huntington's disease.
papers.authors: Vazquez-Sanchez S, Arnold-Garcia O, Chillon-Marinas C, Maimon R, Cui J, McNair K, Dai Y, Jimenez NL, Child DD, Thompson LM, Lopez-Erauskin J, Bintu B, Cleveland DW.
papers.abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) is caused by CAG expansion in the huntingtin gene (HTT), yet how somatic repeat instability and HTT inclusions relate to selective cell loss in the human brain remains unclear. We have developed a multimodal spatial transcriptomics approach that enables the definition of transcriptional programs with subcellular resolution, somatic CAG repeat lengths, and eight other pathology markers, including HTT inclusions, in every cell of intact brain sections. Imaging 428,173 cells in the control and HD cortex revealed the selective vulnerability of layer 5-6 (L5-6) near-projecting (NP) neurons and L6b deep-layer excitatory neurons, which undergo a >50% loss that is closely linked to large somatic repeat expansions (>450 ± 55 CAGs). Intranuclear inclusions were most prevalent at intermediate somatic repeat expansions (250-350 CAGs) and were associated with broader transcriptional changes than somatic repeat expansion alone. These data provide a comprehensive resource and establish a general framework for connecting repeat expansion and protein pathology across diverse cell types.

papers.title: Long-range actin-driven endosymbiont mobility in an animal-algal symbiosis.
papers.authors: Zhong G, Toullec G, Jouneau PH, Decelle J, Prakash M.
papers.abstract: In animal-microbe symbioses, established symbionts are often thought to be confined to a niche and to lose motile appendages such as flagella. Whether this loss implies immobility within the host remains poorly understood. We report long-range, host-driven symbiont mobility in a dinoflagellate-acoel worm symbiosis. Using long-term tracking, fluorescence, and electron microscopy, we find that hundreds of dinoflagellate symbionts (Amphidinium sp., 10-20 μm in size) travel across the body of an acoel worm host (Waminoa sp.) at around 1 μm/s while confined inside a network of ultra-thin (∼200 nm) host parenchymal cells. We show this mobility is driven by host actin machinery, with symbionts moving faster than comparable actin-based transport systems despite confinement. We further show spatiotemporal regulation of symbiont distribution during diel rhythms and regeneration. By characterizing an active, host-cytoskeleton-driven mechanism of symbiont transport, our work expands our understanding of the regulatory strategies by which holobionts maintain dynamic homeostasis.

papers.title: Somatic DNA-repeat expansions initiate distinct yet analogous changes in Huntington's disease cortical and striatal neurons.
papers.authors: Kashin S, Lee WS, McDonald TM, Morris K, Handsaker RE, Mello CJ, Spina L, Reed NM, de Rivera H, Jana SH, Hogan M, Berretta S, McCarroll SA.
papers.abstract: Huntington's disease (HD) affects the neocortex and striatum with different timing, severity, and gene-expression changes. These pathologies have long been proposed to involve different pathogenic mechanisms, with one brain area's degeneration leading to the other's. Striatal neurons degenerate in HD as their huntingtin (HTT) CAG-repeat tracts expand somatically beyond 150 CAGs. Here, we find that cortical pyramidal neurons in HD undergo biological changes analogous to those in striatal neurons-the same sequence of pathological phases, with toxicity also commencing at ∼150 CAGs but then changing their gene expression in distinct ways. Pyramidal neurons' precise molecular identities, rather than their areal or laminar locations, appeared to determine the extent of this somatic DNA-repeat expansion, which varied up to 20-fold among pyramidal neuron subtypes. Cortical and striatal neurons also shared a key pathological feature: nuclear inclusions of aggregated HTT protein in those nuclei with expansions well beyond 150 CAGs.

papers.title: Inflammatory memory primes the intestine for enhanced regenerative potential.
papers.authors: Arozamena B, Moraitis I, Mularoni L, Wienskowska O, Taelman J, Stefanovic M, Modolell Farré I, Guedea F, Díaz M, Guiu J.
papers.abstract: How do inflammation and activation of the regenerative genetic program affect intestinal epithelial cell behavior and shape responses to future injuries? Following injury, which typically induces intestinal stem cell (ISC) death, regeneration occurs via the proliferation of surviving ISCs and via cellular plasticity through dedifferentiation of progenitors and committed cells. While inflammation and cellular plasticity are hallmarks of regeneration, its long-term effects on epithelial cell behavior are not well understood. Using single cell multiomics, we demonstrate that inflammatory exposure and cellular plasticity imprint a lasting transcriptional and epigenetic memory on ISCs and their progeny, priming them for enhanced repair after subsequent injuries. Mechanistically, we identify IFN-γ as a critical driver of this primed regenerative state. These findings uncover how prior inflammation reprograms regenerative capacity, with implications for tissue resilience and disease susceptibility.

papers.title: Single-cell landscape of human adipose tissue reveals THBS1 as a potential driver of fibro-inflammation in metabolic disease.
papers.authors: Jung J, Park ES, Lee NK, Lee JJ, Juang U, Huang Q, Park YS, Kim HJ, Kim JK, Oh TJ, Suh JM, Kim JB, Moon JH, Kim JK, Choi SH.
papers.abstract: The cellular complexity of adipose tissue plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of metabolic disease; however, mechanisms underlying adipose dysfunction remain poorly understood. Here, we constructed a single-nucleus and bulk transcriptomic atlas of human visceral adipose tissues from an ethnically homogeneous cohort with defined metabolic states: lean with normal glucose tolerance, obesity, and obesity with type 2 diabetes. Single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) revealed a fibro-inflammatory subpopulation of adipose stem cells and adipocytes characterized by high THBS1 expression, which were enriched in individuals with obesity and obesity with type 2 diabetes compared to lean controls. Through complementary in vitro (human primary ASCs, THP-1 macrophages, and Matrigel-captured mature adipocytes), ex vivo (mouse and human visceral adipose tissue explants), and in vivo (gain-of-function and antibody-mediated neutralization) experiments, we demonstrated that THBS1 promoted adipose fibrosis and inflammation via macrophage-mediated TGFβ activation, impairing adipogenesis and adipocyte function. Inhibition of THBS1 attenuated fibro-inflammatory features in metabolically dysfunctional adipose tissues. Moreover, THBS1 levels in plasma and adipocytes correlated with metabolic traits, including BMI and HbA1c. Collectively, our study provides a cellular atlas of human visceral adipose tissues across metabolic disease states and identifies THBS1 as a key pathogenic driver and potential therapeutic target.

papers.title: Deep sequencing of 3,367 maize genomes uncovers substantial contribution of rare variants to agronomic traits.
papers.authors: Huang L, Bian C, Xin B, Zhang X, Lu Q, Yue Y, Li Y, Zeng R, Liu X, Fan X, Wang T, Wang Y, Cao J, Zhang J, Wu J, Lin Z, Zhao J, Cheng W, Gao S, Chen Y, Lu Y, Yang J, Liu W, Chen Z, Sun H, Lu X, Xue J, Yang S, Liu Q, Chen J, Zhao H, Zhao H, Song W, Lai J.
papers.abstract: Rare variants are highly abundant, yet their genome-wide contributions to agronomic traits remain elusive in plants. Here, we performed deep whole-genome sequencing of 3,367 diverse elite maize inbred lines, uncovering 75.3 million variants, of which 79.2% were rare. Overall, we identified 411 independent association signals for 10 agronomic traits, including 359 attributable to globally rare variants, with rare variants showing effect sizes approximately 2.4 times those of common variants. Frequency-stratified genome-based restricted maximum likelihood (GREML) analyses indicated that rare variants captured a substantial proportion of phenotypic variance for traits under strong adaptive selection, consistent with the allele frequencies of trait-associated variants shifting from common in tropical to rare in temperate maize. Complementing conventional variant-level genome-wide association studies (GWAS), gene-based tests identified an additional 94 candidate gene-trait associations. Our study highlights rare variants as important components of the genetic architecture of complex agronomic traits in maize and provides much-needed resources for future functional studies and breeding.

papers.title: Autologous Anterior Lens Capsule as an Intrascleral Spacer in Deep Sclerectomy: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
papers.authors: Einollahi N, Doozandeh A, Rezaei J, Hatami M, Alborzi K, Hassanpour K, Khorrami Z, Yazdani S.
papers.abstract: Objective To compare deep sclerectomy (DS) combined with phacoemulsification (PE), with versus without an autologous anterior lens capsule spacer. Design Prospective, randomized, parallel-group clinical trial. Methods Sixty eyes of 60 adults with medically uncontrolled glaucoma and visually significant cataracts underwent PE-DS with an autologous anterior capsule spacer (Spacer group) or PE-DS alone (Control group). Follow-up was at least 12 months. The primary outcome was change in intraocular pressure (IOP) from baseline through 12 months. Secondary outcomes included glaucoma medication use, surgical success according to prespecified IOP-based criteria, and adverse events. Results Baseline IOP was similar (25.14 ± 9.62 vs 23.77 ± 5.18 mmHg) and both study groups had significant IOP reduction at all visits. IOP was significantly lower in the spacer group at month 6 (11.90 ± 1.82 vs 13.13 ± 2.20 mmHg; P = 0.022) and month 12 (12 ± 2.20 vs 13.29 ± 2.68 mmHg; P = 0.042). Medication use was lower in eyes with an autologous spacer at months 6 (0.14 ± 0.45 vs 0.48 ± 0.85; P= 0.063) and 12 (0.29 ± 0.66 vs 0.68 ± 1.04; P =0.094). Under stringent success definitions, survival favored the spacer (e.g., Definition C: IOP≤12 mmHg: 47.5% vs 15.5%; log-rank test P = 0.025). Conclusions and relevance Adding an autologous anterior capsule spacer during PE-DS was associated with lower IOP at 6 and 12 months and higher cumulative success under stringent IOP thresholds. Medication use was lower in the spacer group, although the between-group differences showed a trend toward statistical significance.

papers.title: Time Course of Resolution of Diabetic Macular Edema by Sustained Suppression of VEGF-A with the Port Delivery Platform with Ranibizumab.
papers.authors: Rustam Z, Khanani AM, Mojumder O, Huddleston S, Scott M, Marcus DM, Kapoor KG, Whitaker S, Awh CC, Walden L, Clark WL, Saini AM, Graff J, Miranda MC, Lin A, Blotner S, Rabena M, Gune S, Campochiaro PA.
papers.abstract: Purpose To determine the incidence of poor responsiveness to VEGF-A suppression in eyes with diabetic macular edema (DME) by evaluating the effect of continuous delivery of ranibizumab via the Port Delivery Platform with ranibizumab (PDS) in individual patients enrolled in the Pagoda clinical trial. Design Retrospective analysis of prospective clinical trial data SUBJECTS: DME patients enrolled in Pagoda (NCT04108156). Methods Change in central subfield thickness (CST) and best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) over time was evaluated for the adjusted intent-to-treat (aITT) population in the Pagoda trial. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) images obtained at each visit were analyzed for 56 PDS subjects from 8 sites to determine the time course of changes in intraretinal and subretinal fluid. Main outcome measures CST, BCVA, and time to resolution of edema. Results In the aITT population the mean duration of follow up was 107.7 weeks in the PDS arm (n=272) and 100.7 weeks the IVT-PDS arm (n=238). The percentage of eyes with CST improvement into the normal range (≤325 µm) by the last visit was 87.9% in the PDS group and 85.3% in the IVT-PDS arm with mean time to normalization of 21.3 weeks and 20.6 weeks, respectively. All eyes in both arms showed reduction in CST over time although some exhibited periods of CST fluctuation and a few in each arm showed initial improvement followed by worsening at last follow up. In the eyes of 56 PDS patients that had detailed analysis of OCTs, normalization of CST occurred in 93% at a median of 17 weeks and elimination of intraretinal fluid in the central 1mm occurred in 84% at a median of 68 weeks. Only 3 of 56 eyes had poorly controlled DME at last follow up. Conclusions Sustained suppression of VEGF-A is sufficient to effectively treat DME in the vast majority of patients, but edema resolution may be slow in some patients giving the false impression of poor response to anti-VEGF-A treatment. In DME, the term unresponsive to anti-VEGF-A treatment should be replaced by slowly responsive.

papers.authors: Battista M, Carbonelli M, Brotto L, Amore G, Coutinho CP, Romagnoli M, Galzignato A, Nucci P, Caporali L, Cascavilla ML, Fiorini C, La Morgia C, Bandello F, Carelli V, Barboni P.

papers.title: In vivo genome-editing therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy: Preclinical studies and first-in-human trial.
papers.authors: Li G, Han F, Wang C, Jin M, Lin J, Zhang H, Yan X, Wang X, Sun X, Yuan Y, Zhang S, Zhang S, Zhu J, Xu Y, Wang Y, Deng Y, Li F, Shi L, Luk A, Wang N, Yang H, Wang J.
papers.abstract: We report the preclinical and early clinical evaluation of in vivo genome editing for Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD), delivered via a single AAV9 vector. In humanized DMD mice, systemic administration achieved targeted genome editing, partial dystrophin restoration, and improved muscle function. In non-human primates, efficient on-target editing was achieved with no dose-limiting toxicity identified under the conditions tested. In an open-label, dose-escalation, first-in-human clinical trial (NCT06594094), post-treatment muscle biopsies provided early molecular evidence of hfCas12Max-mediated genome editing and detectable dystrophin expression in participants with DMD. However, at the higher dose level (1.0 × 10 14 vg/kg), one participant experienced a treatment-related fatal serious adverse event, characterized by marked complement activation and systemic cytokine response shortly after dosing. This work provides initial human proof-of-concept for muscle genome editing while crucially highlighting the critical role of immunologic risks and the narrow therapeutic window of systemic adeno-associated virus (AAV)-CRISPR therapies, underscoring the need to develop safer dosing and immunomodulation strategies.

papers.title: Validation of the University of California, Irvine Corneal Cystine Crystal Score (UCI CCCS): Correlations with Clinical, Imaging, and Symptom Outcomes in Cystinosis.
papers.authors: Rezaei K, Crook T, Shah J, Esfahani PR, Desar N, Wang MJ, Shahraki K, Lee OL, Suh DW.
papers.abstract: Purpose To prospectively validate the University of California, Irvine Corneal Cystine Crystal Score (UCI CCCS), a standardized slit-lamp grading tool, by evaluating associations with objective corneal densitometry, patient-reported symptoms, and visual acuity in a real-world cystinosis cohort. Design Prospective observational cross-sectional study. Participants Seventy patients (140 eyes) with confirmed cystinosis were examined at the 2024-2025 Cystinosis Research Foundation Day of Hope Clinics. Methods All eyes underwent live slit-lamp UCI CCCS grading (0-5). Pentacam Scheimpflug densitometry was obtained in 68 eyes. Two ophthalmologists independently graded patients during the 2025 clinic to assess inter-rater reliability. Patient-reported symptoms, best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), and topical cysteamine treatment data were collected. Linear mixed-effects models accounting for within-patient correlation were used for densitometry and BCVA analyses. Symptom associations were evaluated at the patient level using Kendall's tau-b. Main outcome measures Inter-rater reliability of UCI CCCS; associations with corneal densitometry, patient-reported symptoms, and BCVA. Results Inter-rater reliability was excellent (ICC = 0.995; 95% CI, 0.992-0.996). Linear mixed-effects modeling demonstrated significant associations between UCI CCCS grade and central (p = 0.0016) and anterior corneal densitometry (p = 0.0011) after accounting for within-patient correlation between fellow eyes. Higher UCI CCCS grades were significantly associated with greater photophobia (τ = 0.397, p Conclusion The UCI CCCS is a highly reproducible, clinically practical grading tool associated with objective corneal densitometry and patient-reported symptom burden, while BCVA was not significantly associated with UCI CCCS grade. Longitudinal studies are needed to evaluate treatment responsiveness and prognostic value.

papers.title: High-throughput droplet-based enzymatic DNA methylome profiling enables single-cell resolution of epigenetic heterogeneity.
papers.authors: Li G, Yang Y, Li Z, Wang Q, Wang Y, Guo B, Yang K, Tan M, Li J, Sun J, Zhang G, Xiong S, Zhang M, Zhang Z, Xie Y, Shi Y, Ma X, Ci W.
papers.abstract: DNA methylation is a fundamental epigenetic modification that regulates gene expression, cellular identity, and disease-associated regulatory programs. However, high-throughput single-cell DNA methylation technologies have been limited by DNA degradation, low CpG recovery, and the poor scalability of bisulfite-based methods. Here, we present scEM-seq, a droplet-based single-cell enzymatic methylome sequencing method that integrates barcode ligation within a single emulsification step, followed by postemulsion cytosine-to-uracil conversion. This design substantially reduces DNA loss and enables robust profiling of tens of thousands of single cells per experiment. scEM-seq generates high-quality single-cell methylomes with moderately improved CpG coverage and balanced read utilization compared with other droplet-based microfluidic methods. Applied to peripheral blood mononuclear cells, scEM-seq accurately resolves major immune lineages, and in prostate cancer tissues, it reveals diverse malignant cell states and patient-specific epigenetic and copy number architectures. scEM-seq enables scalable single-cell dissection of epigenetic heterogeneity across diverse biological and disease contexts, broadening the scope of DNA methylation-based studies into cellular regulation and disease.

papers.title: NAD + metabolic restoration resolves the inflammation-immunocompetence trade-off in lung graft-versus-host disease.
papers.authors: Li J, Zhou Z, Qi J, Zhang F, Zhang Z, Li X, Jiang S, Li X, Wang L, Xie X, Chen J, Zeng K, Han Y, Jiang J, Ye M.
papers.abstract: Chronic lung graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) after allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (allo-HSCT) remains difficult to treat, and broad immunosuppression increases infection risk. Single-cell profiling of bronchoalveolar lavage from bronchiolitis obliterans lesions revealed collapse of an epithelial nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD + ) metabolic axis with pathogenic immune-epithelial remodeling, nominating NAD + restoration as an entry point. Because free NAD + is poorly cell-permeable and rapidly consumed, we engineered CaNAD + -PGB-LiP (CNAPL), a high-payload NAD + nanomedicine enabling direct intracellular replenishment. In murine allo-HSCT GVHD, CNAPL improved clinical scores and survival, reduced vascular and epithelial injury, and curtailed hyperinflammation and effector overactivation across GVHD target organs. Unlike immunosuppression, CNAPL preserved phagocytosis, NK/NKT cell (natural killer/natural killer T cell) cytotoxicity, and T cell memory. In posttransplant influenza or Klebsiella infection, CNAPL maintained pathogen control without rekindling GVHD, decoupling inflammation control from infection susceptibility. This metabolism-centered, host-directed strategy restores immune-tissue homeostasis and provides a practical translational path for durable lung GVHD control with preserved antimicrobial defense.

papers.title: Benchmarking segmentation methods for spatial transcriptomics.
papers.authors: Martínez-de-Morentin X, Khan SA, Maillo A, Lehmann R, Kiani NA, Lagani V, Gomez-Cabrero D, Tegner J.
papers.abstract: Cell segmentation is a critical yet under-standardized step in spatial transcriptomics, directly affecting cell identity assignment, spatial organization and downstream biological interpretation. Despite rapid advances in spatial transcriptomics technologies, systematic evaluations of segmentation methods across platforms and biological contexts remain limited. Here we benchmark 11 image-based, transcriptomics-based and multimodal segmentation methods across 15 datasets generated by 5 spatial transcriptomics technologies, spanning 12 human and mouse tissue types. We introduce biologically informed evaluation metrics that quantify segmentation quality, transcript recovery, cell composition, morphology, expression purity and spatial organization. Benchmarking reveals substantial variation in performance across datasets, technologies and evaluation criteria, highlighting trade-offs among segmentation completeness, transcriptomic fidelity and biological interpretability. Cross-technology analyses further demonstrate that segmentation choice critically shapes downstream analyses, including cell-type specificity, transcript contamination and ligand-receptor inference. Together, our unified Nextflow pipeline provides a scalable foundation for standardized evaluation of segmentation and method selection in spatial transcriptomics.

papers.title: Taurine lowers inflammaging by regulating the NLRP3 inflammasome in macrophages.
papers.authors: Guan C, Ryu S, Dong M, Zhu Y, Maeda R, Youm YH, Mohanty S, Kim HH, Orliaguet L, Dlugos T, Smith SR, Ravussin E, Onyuru J, Hoffman HM, Siebel S, Wang A, Wang Y, Kluger Y, Shaw AC, Kanneganti TD, LeBrasseur N, Sugiura Y, Dixit VD.
papers.abstract: Whether a decline in taurine drives aging is debated, and despite high millimolar intracellular concentrations, its function as a potential guardian of cytosolic homeostasis is unclear. Here, we show that aging increases circulating taurine concentrations in humans and mice. Further elevating taurine in aged mice enhances health span, engaging anti-inflammatory pathways previously linked to youthfulness, and reduces mortality from sepsis and inflammasome-mediated inflammation, suggesting an enantiostatic response. Mechanistically, diverse NLRP3-specific "danger signals" induce taurine efflux from macrophages as a proximal step to activate the inflammasome and the resultant pyroptosis. Taurine restoration in macrophages prevents NLRP3-induced trans-Golgi network disassembly, thereby suppressing NLRP3 inflammasome activation. Conversely, lowering taurine biosynthesis combined with reduced bioavailability in macrophages exacerbated inflammasome activation. In humans, sustained caloric restriction elevates adipose tissue taurine and is accompanied by lower inflammation. Together, we identify taurine as an immunometabolic rheostat that links danger sensing to NLRP3 inflammasome activation, suggesting taurine-based strategies to alleviate inflammaging and inflammasomopathies.

papers.title: Cell-state-specific metabolic networks govern ferroptosis versus apoptosis in small cell lung cancer.
papers.authors: Kim JW, Bebber CM, Dai Y, Bopp S, Edenhofer A, Li AM, Rösner T, Berning L, Yang M, Leak LB, Stroh J, Shrestha B, Abdallah AT, Prymidis D, Olivos HJ, Baron M, Nguyen T, Shue YT, Nishiga Y, Drainas AP, Chaikovsky AC, Szylo K, Li Y, Kang YP, Manoj P, Villalonga AQ, Rudin CM, DeNicola GM, Dixon SJ, Frezza C, Ye J, von Karstedt S, Sage J.
papers.abstract: Cellular heterogeneity and plasticity are hallmarks of cancer that contribute to tumor growth and therapy resistance. Here, we investigated metabolic heterogeneity in small cell lung cancer (SCLC), an aggressive cancer type with considerable plasticity between neuroendocrine (NE) and non-NE cellular states. Through integrated transcriptomic and metabolomic analyses, we identified a universal dependency on exogenous cysteine/cystine (Cys) across all NE/non-NE SCLC cell states. Notably, NE and non-NE cells with low ASCL1 transcription factor levels underwent ferroptosis upon Cys depletion, whereas ASCL1 high cells underwent apoptosis while remaining resistant to ferroptosis. This ferroptosis resistance was driven by the direct transcriptional activation of GCH1 by ASCL1, resulting in increased levels of the antioxidants BH4/BH2. Accordingly, combined Cys depletion and inhibition of BH4/BH2 synthesis reduced tumor growth in patient-derived xenografts. These findings demonstrate that metabolic state influences cell-death susceptibility in SCLC and provide a rationale for therapeutic strategies that exploit these metabolic differences.

papers.title: Perforin triggers iron-induced mitochondrial damage to drive ferroptosis and anti-tumor immunity.
papers.authors: Bell HN, Nair K, Tison K, Liao P, Lei H, El-Derany MO, Yisimayi A, Zhang H, Rebernick R, Wang W, Adachi Y, Castillo C, Das NK, An J, Sutton VR, Lin X, Lin H, Wang X, Li Y, Vatan L, Aboud A, Wei S, Gijon M, Goodwin S, Shah YM, Kryczek I, Trapani JA, Barroso M, Lieberman J, Zou W.
papers.abstract: Cytotoxic CD8 + T cells and natural killer cells are critical effectors of anti-tumor immunity. Cytotoxic lymphocytes eliminate tumor cells by releasing perforin (Prf1), a pore-forming protein that enables granzymes (Gzms) to enter target cells and trigger both caspase-dependent and -independent cell death. Here, we uncover a previously unrecognized, Gzm-independent function of Prf1. We find that Prf1 directly induces tumoral ferroptosis, an iron- and lipid-dependent form of cell death. Mechanistically, Prf1-mediated pore formation drives endocytosis of the transferrin receptor, which increases cellular iron uptake. Prf1 promotes the formation of endosomal-mitochondrial contacts, which leads to mitochondrial iron accumulation, mitochondrial dysfunction, and tumor cell ferroptosis. Dietary iron supplementation suppresses tumor progression in murine tumor models in a Prf1-dependent manner. Higher Prf1 expression correlates with improved survival and enhanced response to immune checkpoint blockade in patients with cancer. These findings define a Gzm-independent function of Prf1 as a direct executioner of cancer cell death through ferroptosis.

papers.title: Morgagnian Cataract: Clinical Features, Surgical Management, and Outcomes.
papers.authors: Kang S, Wallace RT, Gedde SJ, Borie CM, Ansari ZA, Vazquez LE, Galor A, Williams BK, Yoo SH, Theotoka D.
papers.abstract: Purpose To characterize the clinical features, surgical management, and outcomes of Morgagnian cataracts. Design Retrospective clinical cohort study. Subjects Fifty eyes of 50 adults diagnosed with Morgagnian cataracts at a tertiary academic referral center in the United States from October 2015 through August 2026. Methods Medical records were reviewed for demographic characteristics, ocular findings, imaging, surgical management, intraoperative complications, intraocular lens (IOL) fixation, postoperative complications, best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA), and intraocular pressure (IOP). Main outcome measures Surgical management, intraoperative complications, postoperative BCVA, and IOP. Results Presenting BCVA was hand motions or worse in 43/50 eyes (86%). Mean presenting IOP was 25.8 ± 16.2 mmHg. Lens-induced IOP elevation was present in 24/50 eyes (48%), lens-induced glaucoma in 19/50 (38%), and zonular weakness in 18/43 (42%). Surgery was performed in 40/50 eyes (80%). Phacoemulsification was initially attempted in 30/40 eyes (75%), manual small-incision cataract surgery in 5/40 (13%), and pars plana lensectomy with vitrectomy in 5/40 (13%). Intraoperative complications occurred in 14/40 eyes (35%), including posterior capsule rupture in 8/40 (20%); overall, 16/40 eyes (40%) received an in-the-bag IOL. Mean BCVA improved from 2.39 ± 0.58 logMAR preoperatively to 0.68 ± 0.81 logMAR at the last follow-up (paired analysis; P Conclusions Morgagnian cataracts were associated with profound visual loss, pressure-related complications, and zonular weakness, with substantial intraoperative risk. Despite this complexity, half of the operated eyes achieved BCVA of 20/40 or better. IOP decreased after cataract extraction in the setting of continued medical therapy in many eyes. These findings support careful preoperative assessment, counseling regarding capsular and zonular complications and potential alternative IOL fixation, and an individualized surgical strategy. However, the retrospective design, modest sample size, and variable follow-up limit interpretation, while the tertiary referral setting may limit generalizability.

papers.title: Membranous Conjunctivitis in Acute and Chronic Graft-Versus-Host Disease: Longitudinal Ocular Outcomes.
papers.authors: Zhao AT, El Jurdi N, Cousineau-Krieger C, Vitale S, Zeller K, Hyder M, Childs R, Arnold DE, Kang EM, Dimitrova D, Carmody E, Rechache K, Kanakry JA, Pavletic SZ, Kanakry CG, Magone MT.
papers.abstract: Purpose To characterize longitudinal ocular surface outcomes and survival in a contemporary cohort of patients with membranous conjunctivitis (MC) after allogeneic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT). Methods Retrospective review of serial ocular assessments performed on patients from baseline through 12-18 months post-HCT as part of the transplant clinical trials at the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Clinical Center. These exams included ocular symptoms, Schirmer's test (ST), conjunctival redness (CR), tear breakup time (TBUT), and corneal staining (COS) and fibrosis assessment. Survival was analyzed from HCT and MC diagnosis. Results MC occurred in 32/369 patients (8.6%) and was associated with acute (28.1%) or chronic (65.6%) graft-versus-host disease (GVHD); two patients (6.3%) had isolated MC without systemic GVHD. MC preceded or coincided with systemic GVHD diagnosis in 46.9% of patients. Median time from HCT to MC was 116 days (range 31 to 1126). The most common presenting symptoms were noninfectious mucoid discharge (50%) and foreign body sensation (37.5%). Tear volume declined by 70.2% at MC diagnosis and remained persistently reduced throughout follow-up. CR and COS increased (both P Conclusion Membranous conjunctivitis is a severe inflammatory ocular GVHD phenotype that occurs in both acute and chronic GVHD and is associated with persistent tear dysfunction and conjunctival fibrosis, underscoring the importance of pre-HCT ophthalmic examination and post-HCT surveillance for early recognition and coordinated multidisciplinary management.

papers.title: Sequential diagnosis with language models.
papers.authors: Nori H, Daswani M, Kelly C, Lundberg S, Ribeiro MT, Wilson M, Liu X, Sounderajah V, Carlson JM, Lungren MP, Gross B, Hames P, Suleyman M, King D, Horvitz E.
papers.abstract: We explored the capabilities of frontier language models in sequential diagnosis, a diagnostic paradigm that captures the iterative nature of clinical reasoning. Given a brief clinical presentation, clinicians selectively acquired information to reach a diagnosis, enabling assessment of diagnostic accuracy and workup cost. We developed an interactive benchmark and an artificial intelligence (AI) system that simulates a panel of physicians, continually revising the differential diagnosis and selecting cost-effective tests. Using this benchmark, the system achieved 83.2% accuracy on New England Journal of Medicine clinicopathological conference cases and 80.3% on MIMIC-IV-ED emergency department admissions, outperforming generalist physicians (36.1 and 46.8%, respectively). Although these findings were obtained in a controlled benchmark setting, they highlight the promise of language models for supporting more accurate, lower-cost diagnoses.

papers.title: Natural product biosynthesis by guanidine prenyltransferases in plants and bacteria.
papers.authors: Kolling D, Konzok K, Taser D, Jentsch T, Schwoerer S, Struwe H, Bültemeier A, Freiberg J, Witte CP, Franke J, Luzhetskyy A, Kirschning A, Rudorf S, Koehnke J.
papers.abstract: Guanidine exists almost exclusively as a resonance-stabilized cation, making its direct enzymatic functionalization challenging. We identified the cyanobacterial enzyme NosH, which catalyzes direct prenyl transfer to free guanidine. Structural and mechanistic analyses revealed guanidine activation by a two-aspartate clamp coupled to prenyl-donor binding through a distinct catalytic architecture. Guided by these features, we identified a large family of guanidine prenyltransferases across bacteria and plants. Plant enzymes produced guanidine alkaloids such as galegine in vitro and heterologous expression of a plant ortholog in Nicotiana benthamiana produced galegine in planta, providing a direct enzymatic link to plant-specialized metabolism.

papers.title: Ultrarapid decision-making in an avian brain.
papers.authors: Schmidbauer P, Nieder A.
papers.abstract: Perceptual decision-making is well studied in mammals, but its operation in other vertebrates remains unclear. We show that carrion crows ( Corvus corone ) make deliberate decisions in a classic visual motion discrimination task with unprecedented speed, reporting choices in approximately 235 milliseconds on average, which is roughly twice as fast as has been observed in monkeys or humans and without sacrificing accuracy. Recordings from the pallial endbrain reveal that direction-selective neurons encode the upcoming choice as early as about 70 milliseconds after stimulus onset and about 170 milliseconds before the response, with ramping activity scaling with sensory evidence and converging at response onset. These findings highlight the extraordinary efficiency of avian decision-making circuitry, possibly shaped by evolutionary pressures for rapid visuomotor control.

papers.title: BAK and BAX form a multiprotein complex to drive mtDNA efflux and caspase-independent cell death.
papers.authors: Yang S, Kim H, Liao G, Ta N, Tu HC, Ramani S, Chen CY, Li ZY, Tanno N, Hsieh JJ, Cheng EH.
papers.abstract: The apoptotic regulators BAX and BAK, once activated, form homo-oligomers to trigger mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization (MOMP), activating the apoptosome and caspases. Activation of BAX-BAK without apoptosome activation triggers sustained efflux of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) and caspase-independent cell death. However, the molecular basis of mtDNA efflux remains unclear. We purified a macromolecular complex comprising BAK, BAX, activator BH3-only molecules, voltage-dependent anion channels 1 and 2 (VDAC1 and VDAC2), and prohibitins that released mtDNA from mitoplasts. BAX-BAK activation resulted in VDAC closure, mitochondrial calcium influx, and mtDNA efflux. Loss of VDAC1, VDAC2, or prohibitins prevented BAX-BAK activation-induced mtDNA efflux and caspase-independent cell death without affecting MOMP or mitochondrial inner membrane herniation. These findings support differential regulation of cytochrome c and mtDNA efflux by distinct BAX-BAK complexes.

papers.title: Wireless electrocatalytic closed-loop system for drug-free management of diabesity.
papers.authors: Maity D, Guha Ray P, Buchmann P, Charpin-El Hamri G, Fussenegger M.
papers.abstract: Lifestyle-related type 2 diabetes and associated obesity (diabesity) affect >2.5 billion people worldwide and impose nearly $3 trillion in annual health care costs. We developed an implantable, wirelessly powered electrocatalytic closed-loop health optimization (ECHO) device containing platinum-decorated gold nanoclusters embedded in graphite felt that enabled selective, electrically tunable oxidation of blood glucose to renally cleared gluconate. In type 2 diabetic mice, wireless, low-power activation (0.75 volts, 10 milliamperes) restored glucose homeostasis within 1 hour, shifted metabolism from glucose to lipid utilization, reduced body weight and triglycerides, and increased circulating free fatty acids and ketone bodies without detectable hypoglycemia or adverse physiological, inflammatory, or behavioral effects during 6 weeks of treatment. Coupling this ECHO device to a commercial continuous glucose monitoring system enabled autonomous, smartphone-controlled, drug-free closed-loop management of experimental diabesity.

papers.title: Electronic bound states in the continuum in a two-dimensional metal.
papers.authors: Thinel M, Huang X, Chica DG, Turkel S, Rossi SE, Koay CS, Li H, Mihalyi-Koch W, Samanta B, Holbrook M, Devarakonda A, Nashabeh LM, Georgescu AB, Roy X, Zhu X, Pasupathy AN, Queiroz R.
papers.abstract: Bound states in the continuum (BICs) are quantum states that remain localized despite lying within a continuum of extended, delocalized states. Whereas optical BICs have been realized in photonic systems, achieving electronic bound states embedded in a metallic background remains an ongoing challenge. In this study, we used scanning tunneling microscopy to identify two defect-induced electronic states that remain localized within the metallic continuum of Pd 5 AlI 2 , a two-dimensional van der Waals metal. Our calculations suggest that electron-hopping interference on the decorated checkerboard lattice of Pd 5 AlI 2 gives rise to a (quasi) flat band built from spatially localized eigenstates that are orthogonal to the dispersive continuum. Atomic defects within this frustrated lattice shift the associated flat-band localized states into the metallic continuum, forming robust, symmetry-protected BICs.

papers.title: Imaging electron-hole asymmetry in the quantum melting of generalized Wigner crystals.
papers.authors: Berger E, Arumainayagam M, Dong Z, Schneider L, Wang T, Nichols G, Kahn S, Dutta R, Wang G, Taniguchi T, Watanabe K, Naik MH, Zaletel MP, Wang F, Crommie MF.
papers.abstract: Two-dimensional moiré materials provide a versatile platform to explore phase transitions in strongly correlated systems. Using scanning tunneling microscopy, we imaged the density-driven melting of generalized Wigner crystals (GWCs) and Mott insulators (MIs) in electron-doped, near-60°-twisted molybdenum diselenide bilayers featuring a triangular moiré superlattice. We observed notable electron-hole asymmetry in GWC melting: Hole-doped GWCs yielded interaction-driven disordered states, whereas electron-doped GWCs melted into delocalized liquid-like states. This asymmetry arose from the broken particle-hole symmetry of the moiré superlattice, which produced electron and hole Fermi pockets with different momentum geometries upon GWC condensation. MI states melted without such asymmetry, consistent with the absence of a symmetry-breaking density modulation. This work provides direct visualization of the emergent phases that appear as GWCs undergo quantum melting transitions.

papers.title: Intron retention regulates STAT2 function and associates with immunotherapy response in lung cancer.
papers.authors: Englander RP, Brugiolo M, Devoucoux M, Wu TC, Kostich M, Leclair NK, Walawalkar I, Kang HG, Park S, Marches F, Peeples ME, Chen P, Banchereau J, Yu P, Salner A, Banchereau R, Palucka K, Anczuków O.
papers.abstract: Immunotherapy with checkpoint inhibitors has revolutionized cancer therapy and enabled considerable therapeutic advances for treating various diseases, including lung cancer. However, the molecular determinants of variable patient outcomes remain unclear. Using long-read RNA sequencing, we mapped the landscape of alternative RNA splicing in human primary lung adenocarcinomas. We identified more than 149,000 full-length messenger RNA (mRNA) isoforms, more than half of which were unannotated and many that occurred in immune-related genes, particularly within the type I interferon response pathway. We functionally characterized retained introns in the STAT2 gene that produced altered protein isoforms that regulated immune signaling and interferon responses and correlated with patient survival after anti-programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1) immunotherapy. These findings position alternative splicing as a regulator of tumor immune responses and reveal intron retention in STAT2 as an interferon regulatory axis that correlates with PD-L1 checkpoint inhibitor response.

papers.title: Visualizing symmetry-broken Chern insulators and their quantum melting.
papers.authors: He M, Tsui YC, Peng R, Watanabe K, Taniguchi T, Vafek O, Yazdani A.
papers.abstract: In the presence of a magnetic field, electronic states of moiré quantum materials develop a Hofstadter spectrum that provides a distinctive setting for studying the interplay between band topology and strong electron-electron interaction. Using scanning tunneling microscopy, we studied Hofstadter's states in bilayer graphene aligned with hexagonal boron nitride and directly visualized the formation of interaction-driven symmetry breaking Chern insulators. Our measurements revealed the formation of phases that double, triple, or quadruple the moiré unit cell at fractional filling of the Hofstadter bands as well as states with complex intra-unit cell wave functions. We visualized two distinct quantum phenomena in different Chern states, including quantum melting driven by the appearance and proliferation of topological defects and a quantum transition co-occurring with phase competition and separation.
